query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled thermal treatment to eutectic high-entropy alloys will enhance both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility by promoting the formation of more favorable microstructural features.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloys with dual-phase lamellar colonies and numerous internal boundaries.
generation.conditions: Room temperature and standard atmospheric conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Microstructural features such as grain size and phase distribution.
generation.mechanism: The thermal treatment will refine the microstructure, reduce internal boundary density, and promote ductile phase formation, thereby mitigating microcracking during tensile deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Increased tensile strength and ductility compared to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline.
generation.baseline: Unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloys with known brittleness and limited ductility.
generation.boundary: The treatment must not exceed specific temperature and time parameters to avoid excessive grain growth or phase transformation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature and duration for optimal treatment are not defined, and the response of the material to thermal treatment may vary.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct tensile tests on both thermally treated and untreated samples of eutectic high-entropy alloys.
measurements: Microstructural analysis before and after treatment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally treated samples do not show a statistically significant increase in both tensile strength and ductility compared to untreated samples, the hypothesis is falsified.
